extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and students of moral/philosophical essays (readers of Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted normative principles and prescriptive judgments from Montaigne's essays about methods of education, the nature of belief, and the character of friendship. The page offers practical and philosophical guidance rather than a formal checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize thought over eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine speaking (gloss, outward ornament, words and elocution) is commendable but not as excellent or necessary as understanding and having good thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not spend your whole life on style alone; first seek to understand your own language and the substance of your thoughts. Avoid valuing mere ornament above intellectual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master native and practical languages first
rubrics_metrics.description: One should first understand one's own language and that of neighbours, because most business and conversation lie there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greek and Latin are ornaments of great use, but practical everyday language mastery should not be sacrificed for scholastic display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor immersion and natural use for learning languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical tongues (Latin/Greek) are best learned cheaply and effectively by immersion—continuous use in daily life—rather than by prolonged, tedious formal study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne's father hired a native Latin-speaking tutor who spoke only Latin to the child and imposed a household rule of speaking Latin around him; this produced fluent, natural Latin without grammar drills. Anti-pattern: long rote grammar study that delays other intellectual development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate learning by liberty and delight, not severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should make children relish science and duty by unforced will; it should be carried on in liberty and delight without harsh constraint or severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use play, games (e.g., tossing declensions), pleasant incentives, and gentle methods (even waking by music) to form habit and appetite for knowledge. Avoid violent or punitive methods that produce mere compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use discretion to permit pleasurable reading as a gateway
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing children to read pleasing books suited to their age can whet appetite for more serious study rather than producing aversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne's tutor discreetly permitted his reading of Ovid's Metamorphoses and other enjoyable texts, which led him on to Virgil, Terence, Plautus, and Italian comedies. Anti-pattern: forbidding all diversion and thereby creating hatred of books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rote memorization and overloading by force
rubrics_metrics.description: To do well, do not cram children with learning by lash and rote; such force only makes 'asses laden with books' who keep knowledge without loving it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to lodge knowledge in them by inspiring appetite and affection for learning rather than by compulsion. Anti-pattern: excessive emphasis on themes, rote, whipping, or tears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity and environment matter in language acquisition
rubrics_metrics.description: Discontinuous exposure and institutional practices (e.g., college methods) can corrupt earlier pure language gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent language use; the switch to college practices caused Montaigne's Latin to 'grow corrupt' despite earlier immersion success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical and public exercises are beneficial
rubrics_metrics.description: Acting in plays and public spectacles are useful exercises for youth and civic life; they augment society, friendship, and orderly diversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-governed communities should support sports and spectacles; acting trains presence, voice, gesture, and social engagement. Anti-pattern: condemning all public entertainments or excluding worth-while performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not measure truth and error by your own capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: It is folly and presumption to declare things false simply because they exceed our understanding or seem improbable to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise epistemic humility: recognize the limits of personal capacity, avoid arrogantly circumscribing the powers of God or nature, and refrain from rashly dismissing credible reports. Instead of outright denial, suspend judgment when warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish the impossible from the unusual
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not conflate what is contrary to nature's order (impossible) with that which is merely uncommon or unfamiliar (unusual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom and familiarity shape what seems credible; novelty often provokes inquiry while familiarity breeds complacency. Treat credible testimony with more caution than blanket skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: When testimony is credible, prefer suspension to dogmatic denial
rubrics_metrics.description: Many unlikely things are attested by trustworthy people; if you cannot fully accept them, you should at least leave them in suspense rather than condemn them as impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include reports in ancient annals and saints' miracles; Montaigne recommends caution in immediate rejection and warns against the arrogance of dismissing such accounts outright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about conceding points in religious controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting opponents some disputed articles as 'indifferent' is risky: concessions can embolden the adversary and those 'indifferent' points may be of great importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either fully submit to ecclesiastical authority or not; partial concessions can be strategically and doctrinally dangerous. This is both an epistemic and practical-political warning.

rubrics_metrics.name: True friendship must be voluntary and free from mixed aims
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest perfection of friendship is a voluntary tie, not founded on pleasure, profit, public or private interest, or natural obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendship is nourished by free communication and similarity of manners, parts, and inclinations. Anti-patterns: familial duty, utility, or contractual relations masquerading as friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship is spiritual, temperate, and grows by enjoyment
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike erotic love (which is active, fickle, and satiable), friendship is steady, temperate, equal, and is actually nourished and improved by shared enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendship refines the soul; fruition increases it rather than destroying it. It is a general, constant affection rather than a feverish, intermittent passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marital ties and age disparities hinder perfect friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage is a covenant whose continuance is often forced and entangled with other interests, making perfect, voluntary friendship rare within it; similarly, marked disparities of age or office commonly prevent the parity needed for true friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfect friendship requires parity of soul and freedom of choice; institutional bonds, inheritance issues, and age differences introduce complications that weaken the voluntary intimacy friendship requires.
